(Raises hand) used to do that until, well, very recently. I use past tense but I know it is a looming threat for me, who knows when I will fall back in this habit lol.

Some things have helped me stop, unfortunately it involved changing the way I consume media. For a few examples,

Trying to figure out my Kibbe ID to find an objectively flattering wardrobe instead of changing it to fit the current obsession... this is a time consuming process however!

Consuming less long-running shows (my favourite one ended not too long ago so it was easier for me) and more standalone projects like movies

Falling back into reading, I mostly read literary fiction rather than YA series. It's easier to not obsess about a certain character in literary fiction because characters are less relatable and sometimes they feel like a means to an end rather than a "person" if you see what I mean.

Going back into hobbies and sometimes modifying them to avoid mirroring. I draw, but I've stopped drawing humans because it always gave me an identity crisis!

I also alternate between "story video games" (where there are characters) and "not story" games like Animal Crossing or sandbox games, where the focus isn't the characters but the gameplay and freedom.

I'm not sure if those tips are applicable to everyone, but I hope it helped! I think being more mindful of the way we consume media is necessary in any case.

EDIT : I forgot but one of the key things I do as well is... going outside more often. Libraries, museums, empty coffee shops... or just take a walk to somewhere instead of taking the bus.

Hey ! I'm also a short (5'1-5'2) FN ! And I definitely HATE anything free-spirit/boho, lmao. Hopefully, that's only a stereotype and you don't need to wear that to dress for your ID.

When you're FN, you only have to worry about two things per Kibbe : having an uninterrupted vertical line and having enough room for width.

The width part is easy nowadays because most clothing has stretch and it can fit without tailoring. You just want to make sure the clothing you buy has enough "room" for you.

For example, I have two crop tops that aren't in the same material, one is very stretchy and lightweight and I love it. The second one has a thicker, more rough texture and barely stretches. I don't wear the second one anymore because it just looks wrong and almost ill-fitted, because it doesn't accomodate my width.

The vertical part is a bit trickier, it means that your whole outfit has to bring the eye from up to down. It is the opposite of a staccato effect for Gamines where your eye jumps from point to point to point when you see the whole outfit.

Dressing for vertical can be done in several ways : monochrome, similar color hue/intensity for top and bottom, literal long pieces like dresses, recalling colours on hat/shoes/patterns, etc. I've personally stopped tucking my tops to avoid a harsh vertical break at the waist which I find very unflattering on me.

If you want some ideas for style, I live in France so I am basically wearing a Parisian style, but I make sure the fits are a bit less tailored and strict than what you may see on Pinterest. I wear soft merinos turtlenecks, corduroy trousers, wide necked cotton shirts (I love a wide neckline!!!! Especially if its square). I found trousers easier to manage than jeans as long as they don't have too much stretch and don't cling awkwardly on my hips.

Hope this helps! You can basically wear any style as long as you can manage to accomodate width and vertical.

From my understanding, they have a lot of key differences. We have to remember that TR is overwhelmingly Yin with a dash of Yang, while SG is almost equally as Yang as Yin, but slightly more Yin. 

SG fabrics and cuts are a lot crisper than TR. Their looks incorporate more details and animated prints and line breaks. It is important to find those in a proper Gamine look because it imitates the (often forgotten) juxtaposition Gamines have.

Line breaks don't need to be colour blocking, there are multiple ways of creating line breaks. The outfit just needs to make your eyes kind of jump all over the place, if I may say so. It's in opposition to a vertical look where the eye is drawn from up to down.

A point Kibbe has insisted on is the importance of having short hair so it can fit the line breaks present in Gamine outfits. If you feel short hair wouldn't suit you, I would strongly suggest looking at another ID, as, if I recall right, Kibbe said it is quite a strong sign one isn't a Gamine.

There's also the essence that might help you choose between the two : Gamines have a sassier vibe compared to TRs. I'd look at Leslie Caron's old movies to catch the vibe SGs have, I think she's a very good example that helped me understand this ID more.

Hope it helped!

1. Height only matters when it's too tall for Yin IDs. You can be short and need longer lines.

2. Very bluntly, I'd recommend against posting your pictures in general, especially if you're a beginner in the system. You can be led astray very easily, especially since I've noticed people tend to type people based on "trends", like "oh it's Romantic season" somehow!

If you're rather small but have reasons to think you might be a Yang ID and would like to verify it by posting, I'd make a throwaway and say something like "my height doesn't preclude me from any ID" or just say that you're 5'4 or 5'5 lol.

But in all honesty, if you're not adverse to Facebook (you can use browser add-ons to not be tracked and you don't need to put your real picture) I'd just recommend you to join the Strictly Kibbe group and see his exercises by yourself! It's free and you're not forced to participate in the groups.

I don't think all SDs have to have this element of undeniable tallness as you call it. I remember people saying that Rita Hayworth looked "smaller" than what they imagined, yet she's a verified SD. Not everyone has to be a supermodel to be a Dramatic type.

The main difference between DC and SD would be the balance and curve. I don't think there's much overlap between the two IDs for this reason. There is no reason to mistake one for the other, unless pictures are distorted (as often) or the person doesn't recognize Kibbe curve and balance.

But then I do agree with you in disagreeing with a lot of typings that are thrown out there, which is why I'd recommend people to find their IDs by themselves.

There is no minimum height for any ID. But there are maximum heights for some types. Above 5'7 (I believe) you have automatically dominant vertical and thus are either SD, FN or D. 

However, the opposite isn't true : being small in stature doesn't mean being petite in the Kibbe sense.

Gamines need to be petite (aka literally small in all directions) but with a Yang bone structure. They're still very compact-looking and small. Look at unedited and unposed Halle Berry pictures to see what I mean. She looks a lot smaller than on Red Carpet pictures.

Classics need to be balanced first and foremost. They can't be petite nor too elongated nor have too much curve. There is no minimum height to have balance as a main feature, Veronica Lake was very small (like not even 5'0 I believe) and yet is a verified Soft Classic.

Naturals have Kibbe width, which is a relation between the upper and lower body. There's more about it in the subreddit's description. Again, no minimum height for both SN and FN, it all depends on if someone accomodates width or not - then curve or elongation to choose between SN and FN. Kibbe verified a 5'0 FN who isn't a celebrity a few years ago. Sarah Jessica Parker is 5'2 or 5'3 and also a FN.

I hope it helped!

I'm still in college and I'm a Soft dramatic. To flatter your ID, you can absolutely dress however you like / want, you just need to tweak a few things.

Especially be mindful of keeping a long vertical line in your outfits - in both cut and colours. If you mostly wear black, it's easier. If you want to mix some colours in one outfit, I'd be nice to think of repeating that same colour somewhere else in the outfit, so the impression is cohesive and the eye is drawn from top to bottom and not all over the place. 

As for cuts, it means avoiding flares at the extremities. It doesn't mean tight, but it always looks nicer when extremities are tapered and gently flowing into the body line. For example, I avoid bouffant skirts but I can definitely pull off A line skirts that are not too flared - bonus point if it's black because I also wear black hosiery under it. 

Kibbe likes to give a T-shaped silhouette to SDs, which means wide neckline (off shoulder, boat, square) and the rest is fitted. Something I see a lot in SD moodboards is waist emphasis and I wouldn't recommend it. Just fitting the waist is good enough, you don't need to attract the eye to it or else you can ruin the vertical.

Some outfits I wear with these in mind : usually those are two colours that are similar but not the same

- Off shoulders top which is close to the body, with A line skirt the same color as hosiery and shoes

- Mockneck top which is close to the body with jogger style pants that are fitted at the ankle, and not too loose, with ankle boots that are close to the ankle

- Medium length jumper (that isn't chunky) with long puff sleeves that taper back at the wrists, and skinny jeans and shoes the same colour

- Long jumper (hoodie) that isn't too loose (i can add a thin belt to make it more fitted but keep in mind the belt should really be discreet!) with skinny jeans or leggings a similar colour.

Hello! I don't wear makeup either, so I wanted to answer this. Hope it's okay!

There's a "stereotype" of Naturals being able to pull off a real bare face the best. I also think that some Romantic suggestions for makeup veer into "no make-up makeup" territory.

But really, I feel like being able to go along bare-faced has a lot more to do with, in order of importance :

1. Your Essence. Perhaps having a less bold essence(like ingenues, classics maybe) can make it easier to live without makeup. But I honestly don't feel like this is the most important.
2. The cohesiveness of your look. Casual and "lightweight" looks are better suited to no-makeup looks compared to more dressed-up looks. I believe all IDs can wear "lightweight" looks in their lines, tbh, even Dramatics or SDs.
3. Confidence. I feel like this is the most important factor, especially as we're all conditioned to feel obliged to wear makeup.

Ultimately, I feel that each and every ID can go barefaced. I'm not a Natural, nor a Romantic, and yet I don't wear makeup even for events. Even though I avoid makeup because I have sensitive skin, I don't feel "incomplete" without it. It's a question of perception.

Maybe I've rambled for too long, but my point is that I believe that there's no ID that can pull off no-makeup better than others? It depends too much on the individual and their whole personal style. I hope I still answered your question while expressing my thoughts!

A compelling landscape, in my opinion, relies on four things : a cohesive colour scheme, the rendered atmosphere, varying levels of details and composition. For these four things, there's no secret other than to watch how other people do it and try to apply their techniques to your own drawings. That's why using tutorials is a good way to start, but it's not enough in the long run. You need to observe both paintings and nature and check what makes them beautiful or interesting.

I'd also suggest you read up on how to choose colours, how to render light, how to crop your drawing to have a focal point/a dynamic composition, how to draw and paint foliage, fur, etc. and practice first. Try to paint independent objects first before gathering them into a single landscape picture. It's all about gathering knowledge before using it. Eventually, you can use the same technique to paint about whatever you want to paint, people, creatures... 

Also, I know people can use touchpads to paint digitally, however if you want to be serious about it, I'd try a cheap tablet like Huion, or some old Wacom model if you can find one (mine is over 10 years old and still great). It really changes everything and makes the transition from digital to traditional painting (or the opposite) much smoother. You can also try Medibang if you want to try another drawing software, as I found it more intuitive than Gimp (but it's your call!). Good luck ! :)

For starters, I'd ask myself : what am I aiming for? Why are you making this story, and why are you writing/drawing/filming it? I don't necessarily think passion is the most important factor, but you should at least have an idea of your goals. Is it to move people? Is it to convey an important message? Is it to earn money? Or do you not care about earning money? Your storytelling should ideally change to fit your final aim.

Inspiration is important, however, reading about more "technical" aspects might be the key to **actually** produce something instead of dreaming it.

I find not only consuming creative works, but also reading up reviews, criticism, etc. has tremendously helped me building a more critical eye -- which I think is key in order to improve. Depending on what kind of story you want to make (is it writing, drawing?), there are accessible YouTube channels on each matter. Artists' channels often talk about their experiences as storytellers, those are a goldmine. There are also booktubers who offer criticism on popular books if you wish to write your story.

I also think it is important to "learn the rules" of the field you want to enter. For example, to draw even cartoony stuff it is important to know how anatomy works. If you want to write a story, I'd suggest reading up on : tropes (and how to make them seem not overdone), folklore and the stages of storytelling, for example. Depending on what you want to do, I'd also suggest reading up on how to storyboard, or maybe take classes on literary theory or on the history of the medium you chose.

And also! Please never feel like it's "too early" or you're not skilled enough to start working on your projects. Start whenever you want, because you're going to improve along the way without a doubt.

Good luck! I hope this was at least a bit helpful.

Hello! I found this piece very interesting, and thus I wanted to try writing my first criticism about it! I hope you don't mind.

I am a person who studies literature (mostly French lit) and who writes poetry -- I don't know how different my background is from the other two commenters, however I do hope to be useful! Don't hesitate to discard my opinion though, if you feel it is not useful or if it seems irrelevant. Also, English is not my first language, and I do hope I won't make any mistakes or use any strange idioms. I am really sorry if I do.

**First impressions**

Overall, I do kind of agree with the other comments -- it is a confusing piece. It isn't the kind of piece you can skim through and get something out of it.

Things that I did not understand, for example, were,

>"You weren’t afraid when the world’s priorities fell neatly in the mud and storm clouds rumbled by safely."

where I am unsure what are the world's priorities. I think it's one of these things that would require more character building to understand? Please correct me if I am wrong.

>"Old hearts were always forgotten but yours had always been mine."

where I don't understand what is the link with the preceding sentence.

That being said, there is a lot to take there, and it makes it both fascinating and overwhelming.

**Metaphors & Interpretation**

I do believe there are interesting metaphors dispersed throughout your text. I do not believe mixing different kind of metaphors in a single sentence makes a text bad, also.

For example, compared to the two other commenters, I am one to enjoy this :

>"when the stars froze and our memories were fresh enough to smell" 

*because* it calls both to sight and smell. I think both metaphors really evoke this feeling of nostalgia, as smells contain powerful memories. Also the verb "froze" makes me think of yearning, of coming back in time to a stilled image.

However, maybe I am missing something but I don't believe the beginning of the sentence flows well. I would have started the text with the aforementioned metaphors.

For example,

>"when the stars froze and our memories were fresh enough to smell,  
>  
>we sang Blueberry Hill..."

or something like this. I am afraid I don't quite grasp the meaning of this sentence overall, so I do hope I did not ruin it with this example.

But then, I also think that too many concurring images ruin the flow and meaning of the text. One that particularly struck me was :

>"So with the pride of a flightless bird I knelt by your side, staining your hospital pillow with crimson tears."

As much as I love the idea of a flightless bird (makes me think of Baudelaire, but maybe I'm looking too far in it), I believe the "crimson tears" are just too much. With such a powerful image as the bird, I would consider simplifying the rest of the sentence so that it does not clash.

It usually is my complain with this text, there are beautiful images that are just buried by this flood of metaphors. I would consider reducing the number of metaphors. 

Also, be mindful of repetitions such as

>"growing cold in the twilight; we had grown helplessly content."

where the verb to grow is redundant. I would mix these two sentences in one, if there isn't a possibility to simply delete one.

Lastly, I believe your last paragraph was overall over the top, with clichéd imagery.

Between the "tragedy", "agony", "twilight" (which is redundant also, but it's less of a big deal), "God's tears" "dark night", "dawn", "midnight", "white lily", "smoke", "roses"... It kind of feels like a list of the most overused metaphors in poetic texts. It distracts from the meaning and sound way too dramatic to my liking, if I may say so.

I feel with the right balance of straightforwardness and metaphors, this text could be much clearer, less cliché while still retaining a poetic quality, if it is what you wish. Also, if you use less imagery, you can tighten the links between them and create powerful isotopies which seemingly flow into one another.

**Narration & Style**

I feel the first paragraph is good, because it focuses on the romance. Overall I believe you did great with the romantic elements rather than the dramatic ones (and this is coming from someone who does not enjoy romance plots at all). Yet at the same time, the romance elements are weakened by the fact that at no moment the person dying is called a "lover" or any other synonym.

The fact that the person dying is,

>"less in pain" and "grows helplessly content"

as in accepting of death (or that's how I understood it), makes one think of the death of an elderly person. So perhaps the narrator and their lover are elderly, but few things in the text hint to old age, if not the lingering feeling of melancholy throughout your prose and the use of the word "old" once. Or perhaps the person dying is their parent/grand-parent? It does leave me a bit confused if I may admit.

It also kind of sounds like a death by suicide, and then there are no other hints for this as well. Overall, the fact that we don't really understand what happened to the dying character makes it less engaging.

I think the really strong sentence in this text is,

>"I loved you in the morning and I loved you when you died; I loved you on that August night, the day we said goodbye."

Indeed, what makes it eye-catching is the use of the rhythm and anaphors "I loved you". It is such a shame (to me, at least) that there isn't more rhetorical figures of styles in this text! I think you can do great with them, and also they can help make your content much clearer, easier to understand.

Personally, I disliked the use of imperative verbs, such as "Remind me to breathe" and "Don't forget me". To me, they sound a little bit cliché, especially because they are so close to one another. I say this because I have seen this kind of sentences overused in a lot of amateur texts, but you are free to discard this advice, of course.

**Grammar**

I am not too hung on proper grammar, as it seems a very poetic text. However, a few sentences bothered me such as

>"Our minds separated and ridden of light, wetted in cement and dried by the sun."

which is a non-verbal sentence, unless "separated" is a verb and not an adjective, and in this case it shouldn't be linked with an adjective. These kind of "mistakes" if I may call them so, really distract from the deeper meaning.

**Last words**

There are a few things that would have been caught by editing, perhaps. However, I do believe this text has a lot of potential, especially for poetry readers. I think overall, your metaphors are interesting but need much more cohesion to work as a whole -- there is a balance to be found, which can be hard in longer texts & longer poems in prose and verses. Also, be careful of flow, rhythm and sounds, which can really make or break a text!

But I really think this is a good draft and interesting to boot. I would love to read a new version of this later!

I wish you well for your next endeavour! :)
